topic: Product Owner accountability and decision authority

notes.front: The Nexus Guide says a Product Backlog has one Product Owner who has the “final say”. What is the final say about?
notes.back: The contents of the Product Backlog: the single Product Owner decides what it holds, even when several teams work from it.
notes.explanation: The Nexus Guide states this “as described in Scrum”, so it holds for one Scrum Team as well as for a Nexus.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: A Nexus works off a single Product Backlog, and as described in Scrum, a Product Backlog has a single Product Owner who has the final say on its contents.
notes.example: Like a newspaper editor who hears every reporter’s pitch but alone decides what goes into the edition.

notes.front: The Sprint Goal must be finalised prior to the end of {{c1::Sprint Planning}}.
notes.back: Sprint Planning
notes.explanation: The Product Owner proposes how the product could gain value, and the whole Scrum Team then collaborates to define the goal.
notes.evidence: The Product Owner proposes how the product could increase its value and utility in the current Sprint. The whole Scrum Team then collaborates to define a Sprint Goal that communicates why the Sprint is valuable to stakeholders. The Sprint Goal must be finalized prior to the end of Sprint Planning.

notes.front: Who else may attend Sprint Planning besides the Scrum Team, and for what purpose?
notes.back: Other people the Scrum Team invites, to provide advice.
notes.explanation: The plan itself is still created by the collaborative work of the entire Scrum Team.
notes.evidence: This resulting plan is created by the collaborative work of the entire Scrum Team. The Product Owner ensures that attendees are prepared to discuss the most important Product Backlog items and how they map to the Product Goal. The Scrum Team may also invite other people to attend Sprint Planning to provide advice.

notes.front: What can artifacts with low transparency lead to, according to the Scrum Guide?
notes.back: Decisions that diminish value and increase risk.
notes.explanation: Important decisions in Scrum are based on the perceived state of the three formal artifacts.
notes.evidence: With Scrum, important decisions are based on the perceived state of its three formal artifacts. Artifacts that have low transparency can lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk.

notes.front: Inspection without transparency is {{c1::misleading and wasteful}}.
notes.back: misleading and wasteful
notes.explanation: Transparency is what enables inspection in the first place.
notes.evidence: Transparency enables inspection. Inspection without transparency is misleading and wasteful.

notes.front: May a Product Owner use processes, techniques and methods that the Scrum Guide does not describe?
notes.back: Yes. Various processes, techniques and methods can be employed within the Scrum framework.
notes.explanation: Scrum wraps around existing practices or renders them unnecessary, and it makes visible how well current techniques work so they can be improved.
notes.evidence: Various processes, techniques and methods can be employed within the framework. Scrum wraps around existing practices or renders them unnecessary. Scrum makes visible the relative efficacy of current management, environment, and work techniques, so that improvements can be made.

notes.front: The Scrum framework is purposefully {{c1::incomplete}}, only defining the parts required to implement Scrum theory.
notes.back: incomplete
notes.explanation: Scrum is built upon by the collective intelligence of the people using it; its rules guide relationships and interactions rather than giving detailed instructions.
notes.evidence: The Scrum framework is purposefully incomplete, only defining the parts required to implement Scrum theory. Scrum is built upon by the collective intelligence of the people using it. Rather than provide people with detailed instructions, the rules of Scrum guide their relationships and interactions.

notes.front: The head of sales and the head of support each insist that their request goes to the top of the Product Backlog. Both needs are real. What should the Product Owner do?
notes.back: A) Weigh both needs and decide the order herself.
notes.choices:
A) Weigh both needs and decide the order herself
B) Ask the Scrum Master to choose between them
C) Put both at the top and let the Developers pick
D) Ask the two heads to vote with other managers
notes.choicesExplained: B: ordering is part of the Product Owner’s accountability, not the Scrum Master’s. C: two items cannot both be first, and it passes the decision on. D: the Product Owner is one person, not a committee.
notes.explanation: The Product Owner may represent many stakeholders’ needs in one Product Backlog; those who want a different order try to convince her.
notes.evidence: The Product Owner may represent the needs of many stakeholders in the Product Backlog. Those wanting to change the Product Backlog can do so by trying to convince the Product Owner.

notes.front: The users of a hospital booking product never attend Sprint Reviews, but their needs keep clashing with the finance team’s. Whose needs may the Product Owner represent in the Product Backlog?
notes.back: D) Those of the users and finance alike, and any other stakeholders.
notes.choices:
A) None: the Product Owner orders only by technical risk
B) Only the stakeholders who attend the Sprint Review
C) Only the finance team, since it funds the product
D) Those of the users and finance alike, and any other stakeholders
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: the Guide does not limit the Product Owner to the stakeholders who attend or pay; it says many stakeholders. A: the Product Owner represents stakeholders’ needs, not only risk.
notes.explanation: The Guide lets the Product Owner represent the needs of many stakeholders in one Product Backlog.
notes.evidence: The Product Owner may represent the needs of many stakeholders in the Product Backlog. Those wanting to change the Product Backlog can do so by trying to convince the Product Owner.

notes.front: Four Scrum Teams build one product in a Nexus. Each team asks to own and order its own part of the backlog. What does the Nexus Guide say?
notes.back: C) There is one Product Backlog with one Product Owner who has the final say.
notes.choices:
A) Each team orders its own part, and the parts are merged later
B) The Nexus Integration Team orders it by vote
C) There is one Product Backlog with one Product Owner who has the final say
D) Each team gets its own Product Owner
notes.choicesExplained: A and D: a Nexus works off a single Product Backlog with a single Product Owner. B: the final say sits with that one Product Owner, not a vote.
notes.explanation: A Nexus works off a single Product Backlog, and that backlog has a single Product Owner.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: A Nexus works off a single Product Backlog, and as described in Scrum, a Product Backlog has a single Product Owner who has the final say on its contents.

notes.front: The chief technology officer disagrees with the Product Owner’s ordering and tells the Developers to follow his order instead. What does the Scrum Guide say?
notes.back: D) The Product Owner’s decisions, seen in the backlog’s content and order, must be respected.
notes.choices:
A) The Developers should follow the more senior person
B) The two orders should be averaged
C) The Scrum Master should decide which order to use
D) The Product Owner’s decisions, seen in the backlog’s content and order, must be respected
notes.choicesExplained: A: seniority does not move the decision; the organisation must respect the Product Owner’s decisions. C: the Scrum Master does not own the order. B: there is one order, the Product Owner’s.
notes.explanation: The Guide says the entire organisation must respect the Product Owner’s decisions for the Product Owner to succeed; the officer can still try to convince her.
notes.evidence: For Product Owners to succeed, the entire organization must respect their decisions. These decisions are visible in the content and ordering of the Product Backlog, and through the inspectable Increment at the Sprint Review.

notes.front: A large product has one Product Backlog. The director proposes two Product Owners with equal say, to share the load. What fits Scrum?
notes.back: B) One Product Owner with the final say, who may delegate work to others.
notes.choices:
A) Two Product Owners, each ordering half of the backlog
B) One Product Owner with the final say, who may delegate work to others
C) Two Product Owners who must agree on every change
D) No Product Owner; the Scrum Teams order it together
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: the Product Owner is one person, not a committee. D: ordering the Product Backlog is part of the Product Owner’s accountability, and the organisation must respect those decisions.
notes.explanation: The Scrum Guide lets the Product Owner delegate Product Backlog work while remaining accountable, and says the Product Owner is one person, not a committee.
notes.evidence: may delegate the responsibility to others. Regardless, the Product Owner remains accountable. For Product Owners to succeed, the entire organization must respect their decisions. These decisions are visible in the content and ordering of the Product Backlog, and through the inspectable Increment at the Sprint Review. The Product Owner is one person, not a committee.

notes.front: Sprint Planning is ending and the Scrum Team still disagrees on the Sprint Goal. The Product Owner suggests starting work and settling the goal on day three. What does the Guide require?
notes.back: A) Finalise the Sprint Goal before Sprint Planning ends.
notes.choices:
A) Finalise the Sprint Goal before Sprint Planning ends
B) Start the Sprint and agree the goal by day three
C) Let the Product Owner set the goal alone later
D) Run the Sprint without a Sprint Goal this time
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: the goal must be finalised before Sprint Planning ends, and the whole Scrum Team defines it. D: every Sprint has a Sprint Goal.
notes.explanation: The Guide sets a clear deadline: the Sprint Goal is finalised within Sprint Planning.
notes.evidence: The Product Owner proposes how the product could increase its value and utility in the current Sprint. The whole Scrum Team then collaborates to define a Sprint Goal that communicates why the Sprint is valuable to stakeholders. The Sprint Goal must be finalized prior to the end of Sprint Planning.

notes.front: A Product Owner has read about a new database and tells the Developers to use it for the next item. What does the Scrum Guide say about this?
notes.back: A) How to build the item is the Developers’ decision alone.
notes.choices:
A) How to build the item is the Developers’ decision alone
B) The Product Owner decides, as she is accountable for value
C) The Scrum Master decides between the options
D) Stakeholders decide at the next Sprint Review
notes.choicesExplained: B: accountability for value does not include telling the Developers how to build. C and D: no one else tells the Developers how.
notes.explanation: The Product Owner can explain what she needs and why, but the “how” sits at the sole discretion of the Developers.
notes.evidence: How this is done is at the sole discretion of the Developers. No one else tells them how to turn Product Backlog items into Increments of value.

notes.front: During Sprint Planning, a Product Owner starts breaking items into tasks and assigning each task to a named developer. What should happen?
notes.back: A) The Developers plan the work themselves.
notes.choices:
A) The Developers plan the work themselves
B) The Scrum Master should assign the tasks instead
C) The tasks should wait for the Daily Scrum
D) Carry on: task assignment is part of ordering
notes.choicesExplained: D: ordering the Product Backlog is not planning how the work gets done. B: no one else tells the Developers how, the Scrum Master included. C: the problem is who plans, not when.
notes.explanation: In Topic Three the Developers plan the work for each selected item, often by decomposing it, at their sole discretion.
notes.evidence: For each selected Product Backlog item, the Developers plan the work necessary to create an Increment that meets the Definition of Done. This is often done by decomposing Product Backlog items into smaller work items of one day or less. How this is done is at the sole discretion of the Developers.

notes.front: The next Sprint touches a new payments regulation that nobody on the Scrum Team knows well. May the Scrum Team invite a compliance specialist to Sprint Planning?
notes.back: D) Yes, to provide advice.
notes.choices:
A) No: only Scrum Team members may attend
B) Only if the specialist joins the Scrum Team
C) Only if stakeholders approve
D) Yes, to provide advice
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: the Guide lets the Scrum Team invite other people. C: the Guide gives the invitation to the Scrum Team, with no approval step.
notes.explanation: Outside advice can inform the plan, which the Scrum Team still creates together.
notes.evidence: This resulting plan is created by the collaborative work of the entire Scrum Team. The Product Owner ensures that attendees are prepared to discuss the most important Product Backlog items and how they map to the Product Goal. The Scrum Team may also invite other people to attend Sprint Planning to provide advice.

notes.front: Every change to the Product Backlog order must wait for a monthly approval board, so lessons from Sprint Reviews sit unused for weeks. What does the Scrum Guide say about this?
notes.back: D) It makes adaptation more difficult, because people are not empowered.
notes.choices:
A) It only matters for the Developers, not the Product Owner
B) It improves transparency, so it is harmless
C) It is fine as long as the board sees every Increment
D) It makes adaptation more difficult, because people are not empowered
notes.choicesExplained: B: making the backlog visible does not help if no one may act on it. C: seeing the Increment is inspection; the rule is about adapting. A: a Product Owner who cannot act is not empowered either.
notes.explanation: A Scrum Team is expected to adapt the moment it learns anything new, which a monthly queue prevents.
notes.evidence: Adaptation becomes more difficult when the people involved are not empowered or self-managing. A Scrum Team is expected to adapt the moment it learns anything new through inspection.

notes.front: A department head hands the Developers a task list each morning and expects them to follow it. The Product Owner sees the team react slowly to what it learns. What is the most likely link, in Scrum terms?
notes.back: B) The Developers are not self-managing, which makes adaptation harder.
notes.choices:
A) The Sprint is too long
B) The Developers are not self-managing, which makes adaptation harder
C) The Sprint Goal is too vague
D) The Product Owner orders the backlog too rarely
notes.choicesExplained: A, D and C: each may matter elsewhere, but the situation described is people being told what to do, which the Guide links to harder adaptation.
notes.explanation: The Guide ties difficult adaptation directly to people who are not empowered or self-managing.
notes.evidence: Adaptation becomes more difficult when the people involved are not empowered or self-managing. A Scrum Team is expected to adapt the moment it learns anything new through inspection.

notes.front: A Product Owner keeps her real priorities in a private spreadsheet, while the shared Product Backlog is out of date. Funding decisions are made from the shared backlog. What is the risk?
notes.back: B) Decisions that diminish value and increase risk.
notes.choices:
A) None, as long as the Product Owner knows the real order
B) Decisions that diminish value and increase risk
C) Only that the Developers lose some time
D) Only a breach of the tool’s access rules
notes.choicesExplained: A: decisions are based on the perceived state of the artifacts, not on what one person knows. C and D: the Guide names a wider harm, to value and risk.
notes.explanation: The funding decisions rest on an artifact with low transparency.
notes.evidence: With Scrum, important decisions are based on the perceived state of its three formal artifacts. Artifacts that have low transparency can lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk.

notes.front: The team reports an Increment as finished, but some parts were never tested. Stakeholders are planning a launch on the strength of it. What should the Product Owner do?
notes.back: B) Make the real state of the work visible to the stakeholders now.
notes.choices:
A) Keep quiet until the launch date is closer
B) Make the real state of the work visible to the stakeholders now
C) Let the Scrum Master raise it at the Retrospective
D) Ask the Developers to test during the launch
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: waiting leaves stakeholders deciding on a misleading picture. D: that does not fix the decision already being made on low-transparency information.
notes.explanation: Artifacts with low transparency lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk, and the launch plan is such a decision.
notes.evidence: With Scrum, important decisions are based on the perceived state of its three formal artifacts. Artifacts that have low transparency can lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk.

notes.front: A Sprint Review shows that a new feature confuses most users. A manager suggests leaving the Product Backlog as it is until the annual planning round. What does the Guide say?
notes.back: A) Adjust as soon as possible to minimise further deviation.
notes.choices:
A) Adjust as soon as possible to minimise further deviation
B) Wait: the annual plan sets the direction
C) Wait until at least three Sprints confirm it
D) Leave it to the next Product Owner
notes.choicesExplained: B, C and D: each delays a known problem; the Guide asks for the adjustment as soon as possible.
notes.explanation: When the resulting product is unacceptable, what is being produced must be adjusted, and quickly.
notes.evidence: If any aspects of a process deviate outside acceptable limits or if the resulting product is unacceptable, the process being applied or the materials being produced must be adjusted. The adjustment must be made as soon as possible to minimize further deviation.

notes.front: A stakeholder objects that the Product Owner’s way of estimating value is “not in the Scrum Guide”, so she must stop using it. What does the Guide say?
notes.back: C) Various techniques can be used within Scrum.
notes.choices:
A) Only practices named in the Guide are allowed
B) Only the Scrum Master may choose techniques
C) Various techniques can be used within Scrum
D) She must replace it with the Guide’s own method
notes.choicesExplained: A and D: the Guide is purposefully incomplete and gives no single method. B: the Guide does not reserve techniques to the Scrum Master.
notes.explanation: Scrum wraps around existing practices and makes visible how well they work, so they can be improved.
notes.evidence: Various processes, techniques and methods can be employed within the framework. Scrum wraps around existing practices or renders them unnecessary. Scrum makes visible the relative efficacy of current management, environment, and work techniques, so that improvements can be made.

notes.front: After three Sprints it is clear that the Product Owner’s chosen way of writing Product Backlog items leaves the Developers confused. How does Scrum help here?
notes.back: A) It makes the practice’s effect visible so it can be improved.
notes.choices:
A) It makes the practice’s effect visible so it can be improved
B) It requires a standard format for items
C) It forbids any technique that fails once
D) It leaves the problem to the Developers
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Guide gives no required format. C: the Guide does not ban techniques; it exposes how well they work. D: creating and communicating items is the Product Owner’s accountability.
notes.explanation: Scrum makes visible the relative efficacy of work techniques so that improvements can be made.
notes.evidence: Various processes, techniques and methods can be employed within the framework. Scrum wraps around existing practices or renders them unnecessary. Scrum makes visible the relative efficacy of current management, environment, and work techniques, so that improvements can be made.

notes.front: A vice-president tells the Scrum Master to cancel the current Sprint. The Product Owner thinks the Sprint Goal is still worth reaching. Who decides?
notes.back: C) The Product Owner, the only one with authority to cancel.
notes.choices:
A) The vice-president, as the most senior person
B) The Scrum Master, who received the request
C) The Product Owner, the only one with authority to cancel
D) The Developers, who do the work
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and D: the Guide gives the authority to cancel to the Product Owner alone; the vice-president can try to convince her.
notes.explanation: Cancellation authority is one of the decisions the Guide reserves to the Product Owner.
notes.evidence: A Sprint could be cancelled if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete. Only the Product Owner has the authority to cancel the Sprint.

notes.front: Mid-Sprint, a stakeholder sends an urgent request unrelated to the Sprint Goal, which is still valid. The Product Owner wants to cancel the Sprint to start it. What fits the Guide best?
notes.back: C) Keep the Sprint and order the request in the Product Backlog.
notes.choices:
A) Cancel, since urgent work always justifies it
B) Swap it in, even if it endangers the Sprint Goal
C) Keep the Sprint and order the request in the Product Backlog
D) Ask the Developers to work overtime on both
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide’s reason for cancelling is an obsolete Sprint Goal, and this one is still valid. B: no changes are made that would endanger the Sprint Goal. D: it still risks the goal.
notes.explanation: No change is made that would endanger the Sprint Goal, and the goal is still valid, so the request is ordered in the Product Backlog instead of cancelling the Sprint.
notes.evidence: No changes are made that would endanger the Sprint Goal

notes.front: Usage data shows that a senior stakeholder’s favourite feature adds no value. The Product Owner is tempted to keep quiet to avoid conflict. What do the Scrum values ask of her?
notes.back: A) Raise it openly: courage to do the right thing.
notes.choices:
A) Raise it openly: courage to do the right thing
B) Keep quiet until the stakeholder asks
C) Remove the feature without telling anyone
D) Let the Scrum Master break the news
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: both hide the work and its challenges from stakeholders. D: it passes a hard conversation on instead of working on the tough problem.
notes.explanation: Courage and openness point the same way: face the problem and be open about it with stakeholders.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Team and its stakeholders are open about the work and the challenges. Scrum Team members respect each other to be capable, independent people, and are respected as such by the people with whom they work. The Scrum Team members have the courage to do the right thing, to work on tough problems.

notes.front: How does a Product Owner delegating Product Backlog work differ from a Product Owner committee?
notes.back: Delegation: others do the work while the one Product Owner stays accountable. A committee shares the role itself, which Scrum rules out.
notes.explanation: The Guide allows the first and forbids the second in the same section.
notes.evidence: The Product Owner may do the above work or may delegate the responsibility to others. Regardless, the Product Owner remains accountable.
